news_title: Czech testing finds Salmonella problem in poultry meat
efet_title: Czech testing finds Salmonella problem in poultry meat
efet_body:
Enhanced testing of poultry meat for Salmonella in the Czech Republic has found the pathogen in a quarter of samples.
The State Veterinary Administration (SVS) stepped up inspections targeting the presence of Salmonella in imported poultry meat at the end of July.
In total, 93 samples of imported poultry products were tested for Salmonella, and the bacteria was confirmed in 23 samples.

news_title: Salmonella Jalapeño Outbreak Ends With 488 Sick in 34 States - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_title: Salmonella Jalapeño Outbreak Ends With 488 Sick in 34 States - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_body:
The Salmonella jalapeño outbreak has ended with 488 people sick in 34 states with 65 hospitalized, according to the
CDC
. That is an increase of two more states, 57 more patients, and eight more hospitalizations since the last update. There were many
recalls
of jalapeño peppers and products made with them. The new states are Hawaii and Iowa.
The case count by state is: Alabama (7), Arkansas (1), California (2), Colorado (132), Florida (1), Georgia (43), Hawaii (1), Illinois (35), Indiana (6), Iowa (1), Kansas (14), Kentucky (2), Louisiana (1), Michigan (5), Minnesota (133), Missouri (9), Montana (8), New Jersey (1), New Mexico (6), North Carolina (6), North Dakota (2), Nebraska (6), Ohio (4), Oklahoma (9), Pennsylvania (2), South Carolina (8), Tennessee (9), Texas (5), Utah (1), Virginia (3), Washington (1), West Virginia (2), Wisconsin (12), and Wyoming (9). Illness onset dates range from June 16, 2026 to August 26, 2026. The patient age range is from less than 1 to 85 years. Sixty-five people have been hospitalized because they are so sick.
Patients were interviewed about what they ate before they got sick. Of the 308 people interviewed, 281, or 91%, reported eating at a Mexican-style restaurant, including Chipotle Mexican Grill and QDOBA. Meal dates ranged from June 14, 2026 to July 29, 2026.
Many sick people were part of illness clusters, which is defined as two or more people who do not live together who reported eating at the same restaurant location, attending a common event, or shopping at the same grocery store. A total of 36 illness clusters were identified at 31 Chipotle restaurants in seven states, and at five QDOBA locations in two states. Commonly reported ingredient items included jalapeño peppers, red onion, cilantro, and avocado.
Whole genome sequencing showed that the DNA from bacteria taken from patient isolates were closely related genetically, which means that people in this outbreak likely got sick from eating the same food. A traceback investigation, based on where patients reported eating during the timeframe of interest found a common grower in Sinaloa, Mexico. They supplied the peppers to Coast Citrus Distributors and were identified as the likely source in this outbreak.
Many of the recalled items have a long shelf life. Please check to make sure you do not have any of the recalled items in your home. If you do, discard them or take them back to the place of purchase for a refund. If you did eat any of these items recently, monitor your health for the
symptoms
of Salmonella food poisoning for the next week. If you do get sick, see your doctor.

news_title: Ingredient Issues: The acceleration of bacon innovations - meat+poultry
efet_title: Ingredient Issues: The acceleration of bacon innovations - meat+poultry
efet_body:
Protein is currently one of the strongest drivers of food innovation. To differentiate, formulators are trying to deliver elevated sensory experiences. Bacon is proving to be an attractive food to meet today’s consumers’ cravings.
“Bacon continues to resonate with consumers because it sits at the intersection of two trends: the desire for high-protein foods and the desire for indulgence,” said Garrett McCoy, senior manager, research, development and applications, Corbion, Lenexa, Kan. “Bacon naturally checks both boxes because it offers familiarity, flavor and versatility across a wide range of applications.”
Premium is trending
Research from Innova Market Insights, The Netherlands, shows continued growth in premium, indulgent and texture-focused meat products. This creates opportunities for manufacturers to differentiate through both flavor and product format, as well as protein sources beyond pork.
“Whether it’s thicker-cut bacon, gourmet pork belly applications, chef-inspired seasoning blends or bacon snacks with more complex flavor layering, consumers increasingly view indulgence as more than just richness,” McCoy said. “They are looking for products that deliver texture, aroma, flavor complexity and an overall eating experience that feels worth the purchase.”
Sidney Brommel, marketing communications research analyst, Kemin Food Technologies, Des Moines, Iowa, said, “Smoke differentiation is being perceived as a premiumization. We see applewood, cherrywood, pecan-smoked, oak-aged smoke and whiskey barrel-smoked as a selling point for premium bacon products.
“There also is a big surge in various limited-time-offering flavor concepts for bacon,” Brommel added. “Just about every major player in the space has offered some new flavors over the past few years.”
Limited-edition Wright Brand Hot Honey Flavored Real Wood Smoked Thick Cut Bacon from Tyson Foods, Springdale, Ark., is a thick-cut pork bacon with a sweet-heat flavor profile. It includes subtle notes of red pepper and vinegar, balanced with honey, garlic and onion.
Hormel Black Label Frank’s RedHot flavored bacon was a recent co-branded limited-time-offering from Hormel Foods, Austin, Minn. These premium thick-cut slices featured a smoke and spice flavor profile.
Convenience complements premiumization. Hatfield, part of family-owned Clemens Food Group, Hatfield, Pa., now offers a fully cooked bacon topping for foodservice. The product is designed to assist short-staffed operators with being more efficient. There’s no raw handling, no cook time and no skilled labor required.
“This clever hack helps operators do more with less,” said Jenny Moyer Murphy, corporate executive chef at Clemens Food Group, Hatfield, Pa. “It opens the door for effortless experimentation with innovative applications — from savory salads to on-trend ‘swavory’ desserts — all without adding extra work to already busy teams. It’s about delivering that essential bacon flavor and texture, efficiently, consistently and deliciously.”
Bacon offers procesors a familiar platform for experimentation and innovation.
|
Source: Donna Berry
Zak Otto, director of protein research and development, R&D, Wixon, St. Francis, Wis., said, “Alternative bacon meat, such as turkey and beef, has become a little more mainstream as well.”
Niman Ranch, Westminster, Colo., recently introduced 100% Grass-Fed and Grass-Finished Beef Bacon. It is pit-smoked and dry-rubbed, which provides a rich, complex flavor profile, according to the company.
“By using the navel, the beef equivalent of pork belly, we’ve achieved that elusive balance of melt-in-your-mouth fat and satisfying chew that bacon lovers crave,” said Andrew Hunter, Niman Ranch’s executive chef.
Bacon jerky remains an underdeveloped meat snack sector. That is likely to change.
“You can go well beyond just smoked or sweet flavors in jerky. Even global flavors could be used,” Otto said. “Flavor combinations like mango habanero or spicy teriyaki can be applied to give a brand a signature flavor. With these various flavor combinations, bacon jerky could be thought of outside of the breakfast daypart, fitting into any time of day.”
Brommel said, “Bacon also has the benefit of being considered keto-friendly. Bacon jerky could lean into the growing protein, meat snack trend and could be flexible in marketing to different lifestyles and diets.”
Pork bacon jerky, compared to other meat jerkies, is highly prone to lipid oxidation. This can lead to the development of rancid flavors.
“It is highly vulnerable as it combines high-fat content, protein, oxygen exposure and extended shelf-life expectations,” Brommel said. “Antioxidant systems should be considered early in bacon jerky development because antioxidants can help stabilize smoke flavor, spice and flavor systems, fat quality and consumer-perceived freshness.”

The outbreak
has been declared over by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A total of 17 confirmed patients were infected in Florida and Georgia, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Illnesses began on dates ranging from May 11 through Aug. 2. Six patients were hospitalized but no one died.
According to the notice of the expanded recall, Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A., San Carlos, Chile, is taking the action because traceback information linked to the frozen organic berries to blueberries that were the subject of the first recall on July 3 when the outbreak was ongoing.
The recall now includes additional lots of Great Value frozen Organic Triple Berry Blend Great Value frozen Organic Blueberries and one lot of Trader Joe’s frozen Organic Mixed Berry Blend.

news_title: Starfish Seafood Cold Smoked Trio Recalled For Possible Listeria - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_title: Starfish Seafood Cold Smoked Trio Recalled For Possible Listeria - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_body:
Starfish Seafood Cold Smoked Trio, which is made from salmon, halibut and trout, is being
recalled
by the New York State Agriculture Commission for possible Listeria monocytogenes contamination. No illnesses have been reported to date in connection with the consumption of this product. The recalling firm is Krasnyi Oktyabr USA of Brooklyn, New York.
The recalled product is Starfish Seafood Cold Smoked Seafood Trio – Salmon, Halibut, and Trout, that is packaged in 8 ounce containers. The lot number that is stamped on the product label is D139149161-153. The best before date for this food is January 21, 12017. The product was sold nationally at the retail level.
The recall was triggered when sampling by the New York State Department of Agriculture and Market food inspectors and subsequent analysis by Food Laboratory personnel revealed the presence of Listeria monocytogenes in some 8-ounce packages of the product.
If you bought this product, do not eat it. You can throw it away in a secure garbage can with a tight fitting lid after first wrapping or double bagging it so other people can’t see it, or you can take it back to the store where you purchased it for a full refund. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after handling this product.
If you ate this item, monitor your health for the
symptoms
of listeriosis, the illness caused by this pathogen, for the next 70 days. That’s how long the incubation period can be, although most people get sick within a couple of weeks. If you do get sick, see your doctor.

news_title: Pasta recall expanded to include all lots sold at Walmart stores
efet_title: Pasta recall expanded to include all lots sold at Walmart stores
efet_body:
Gias Foods of New York, NY, is recalling all lot codes of bettergoods Authentic Italian Lemon Alfredo Fettuccine, because it has the potential to be contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes.
The Authentic Italian Lemon Alfredo Fettuccine was distributed nationwide at Walmart stores. The company previously recalled certain lots of the product, but has expanded the recall to include all product distributed.
No illnesses have been reported to date.
The recalled bettergoods brand Authentic Italian Lemon Alfredo Fettuccine is frozen and packaged in 22-ounce yellow plastic bags with UPC# 194346442706.
The recall was the result of a routine sampling program conducted by Washington State Department of Agriculture and Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, which revealed that the finished products may contain the bacteria. The company has ceased the distribution of the product as FDA and the company continue their investigation as to what caused the problem.
About Listeria infections
Food contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes may not look, smell or taste spoiled but can still cause serious and sometimes life-threatening infections. Anyone who has eaten any of the recalled
product and developed symptoms of Listeria infection should seek medical treatment and tell their doctors about the possible Listeria exposure.
Also, anyone who has eaten any of the recalled products should monitor themselves for symptoms during the coming weeks because it can take up to 70 days after exposure to Listeria for symptoms of listeriosis to develop.
Symptoms of Listeria infection can include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache, and neck stiffness. Specific laboratory tests are required to diagnose Listeria infections, which can mimic other illnesses.
Pregnant women, the elderly, young children, and people such as cancer patients who have weakened immune systems are particularly at risk of serious illnesses, life-threatening infections, other complications and death. Although infected pregnant women may experience only mild, flu-like symptoms, their infections can lead to premature delivery, infection of the newborn, or even stillbirth.

There have been no confirmed reports of illness or injury due to consumption of these products. Anyone concerned about illness or injury should contact a healthcare provider.
FSIS is concerned that some product may be in consumers’ pantries. Consumers who have purchased these products are urged not to consume them. These products should be thrown away or returned to the place of purchase.

Gias Foods, Inc., is expanding a previous recall to now include every lot code of Bettergoods brand Authentic Italian Lemon Alfredo Fettuccine over fears the product could be contaminated with listeria, an alert from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said on Thursday.
The frozen recalled pasta was distributed across the country to Walmart stores. All lot code numbers are now being recalled, and the product is packaged in 22-ounce yellow plastic, with a UPC number of 194346442706.
There have been no reported illnesses related to the recalled pasta, the alert says.
Read More
on
News
Numerous recalls have been issued this year across the country due to the potential for damage, foodborne illness, contamination, lack of inspection or undeclared food allergens. Recently, federal officials also announced a recent recall from Star Meat Delivery Inc. impacting about 167,639 pounds of
raw beef, pork and goat
because the goods were produced without federal inspection.
When reached by
Newsweek
for comment, a communications representative for Walmart said, "Safety is a top priority. When notified of recalls, we move quickly to remove the impacted products from our stores and implement a sales block at registers and online. We are working closely with our supplier, and customers who have this should discontinue use and follow the recall instructions."
Newsweek
reached out to Gias Foods, Inc., via email Friday for additional information.
...
What To Know About the Recall
According to the alert,
the recall followed routine sampling by both the Washington State Department of Agriculture and the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, which flagged that the finished product could contain the bacteria.
"The company has ceased the distribution of the product as FDA and the company continue their investigation as to what caused the problem," the alert added.
Last month, the product was given
a Class I designation. The FDA describes Class I as "a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death."
People who have purchased the recalled frozen pasta are urged to return it to the original place of purchase for a refund. Consumers with additional questions may contact the company via email at
sales@giasfoods.com
, the alert says.
The FDA warns that
Listeria monocytogenes
is an organism that could potentially cause serious and sometimes fatal infections in people with weakened immune systems, those who are frail or older adults, and children. It could also cause miscarriages or stillbirths in pregnant women and short-term symptoms for healthy people could include high fever, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, severe headache and stiffness.
Recall Concerns and Foodborne Illness in 2026
The latest recall update impacting the frozen pasta comes amid heightened fears and attention to foodborne illnesses and recalls,
including national cases of salmonella
and
cyclospora.
The largest case involving cyclospora this year was in connection with iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) announced
last month that the outbreak was over
after thousands were sickened nationwide.
Similarly, a recall of fresh jalapenos over salmonella concerns prompted additional recalls impacting dips, salsas and other prepared foods. As of Friday, nearly 500 people have been reported sick and 65 hospitalized,
according to the FDA.
Keith Schneider, professor of food safety at the UF Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, said in a release sent to
Newsweek
last month when asked why some recalls involve very large companies or well-known grocery stores, "Large companies distribute enormous amounts of food, so problems involving those products are more likely to be detected."
Schneider added, "Imagine one supplier distributes a million units of a product. If there is a contamination problem, there is a much greater chance that multiple people will become sick and that health officials will see a pattern. A small farm selling a few dozen units may have the same contamination rate, but if only one person becomes sick, that illness may never be connected to the farm or producer. That doesn't mean a large food company is necessarily less safe. Sometimes it simply means the scale of its distribution makes a problem easier to see."

news_title: Salmonella outbreak traced to jalapeños has ended
efet_title: Salmonella outbreak traced to jalapeños has ended
efet_body:
The CDC has called an end to the outbreak of Salmonella Javiana infections traced to imported jalapeño peppers.
A total of 488 people across 34 states were infected with the outbreak strain. There were 65 hospitalizations but no deaths, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The patients ranged in age from less than 1 to 85 years old, with a median age of 31. Illnesses started on dates ranging from June 16 to Aug. 26, with the peak day being July 5 when 38 people fell.
There were likely many more sick people than reflected in the patient count. This is because some people do not seek medical treatment and others are not tested specifically for Salmonella. The CDC estimates for every confirmed patient in a Salmonella outbreak there are 29 who go undetected.
Traceback and epidemiological evidence showed that fresh jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, and distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors were the source of the pathogen. The company recalled its whole peppers and its downstream customers who used the peppers in a variety of products
issued recalls
, according to the Food and Drug Administration.
A total of 36 illness clusters were identified at 31 Chipotle Mexican Grill locations in seven states and five QDOBA locations in two states. Commonly reported ingredient items included jalapeño pepper, red onion, cilantro, and avocado. Of the 308 people interviewed, 281 reported eating at a Mexican-style restaurant before their illness, including Chipotle Mexican Grill and QDOBA, with meal dates ranging from June 14 to July 29.
As part of the outbreak investigation, FDA staff inspected a common Mexican distributor who was identified by traceback. The FDA did not name that distributor.
The inspection included observing operations, reviewing records, and sample collection. At the time of inspection, no jalapeños were available for sampling. FDA collected environmental samples which were all reported as negative for Salmonella. FDA was unable to determine a route or source of contamination for this outbreak.

news_title: Albertsons appoints interim CFO - meat+poultry
efet_title: Albertsons appoints interim CFO - meat+poultry
efet_body:
BOISE, IDAHO – Cody Perdue has been named interim chief financial officer at Albertsons Cos. He currently is senior vice president of treasury, investor relations and risk management and will continue to oversee those functions.
He succeeds Sharon McCollam, who is retiring as president and CFO and will remain with the company in an advisory capacity through February. A search for her permanent replacement is underway.
“Cody is a highly respected finance leader with a deep understanding of Albertsons and a strong record of helping guide our financial strategy,” said Susan Morris, chief executive officer of Albertsons Cos. “His experience across treasury, investor relations, financial reporting and risk management, together with the relationships he has built throughout the organization and with the investment community, make him well suited to lead the finance function during this transition.”
Perdue joined the company in 2013 and has held several finance and accounting leadership roles of increasing responsibility. Prior to Albertsons, he worked at Deloitte and Touche LLP.
“Cody has been my right hand and a trusted partner to the entire leadership team,” said McCollam. “Throughout his career at Albertsons, he has been at the center of the company’s most significant strategic and financial transactions. He is a disciplined and thoughtful financial leader with excellent judgment, and I look forward to working with him to ensure a seamless transition.”

news_title: USDA grant supports Farm Creek Meats expansion plans - meat+poultry
efet_title: USDA grant supports Farm Creek Meats expansion plans - meat+poultry
efet_body:
DUCHESNE, UTAH – Farm Creek Meats, a family owned and operated meat processing facility in Duchesne, Utah, received a $200,000
Value-added Producer Grant
from US Department of Agriculture Rural Development.
The grant will help Farm Creek Meats expand its customer base and strengthen its retail presence to increase overall sales, the agency said. The working capital funds will be used to broaden product offerings, support production capacity and enter new markets. Additionally, the investment will also enhance Farm Creek’s ability to meet growing demand of locally raised and processed meat products, improve operational stability and position the company for long‑term growth and profitability.
“We are extremely grateful to USDA Rural Development for selecting Farm Creek Meats for this Value-Added Producer Grant,” said Douglas Reid, Farm Creek Meats owner. “As a producer-owned, vertically integrated meat company in rural Utah, this award gives us the opportunity to take what we raise and produce here at home and create higher-value products that can compete on a national level.
“This funding will help us bring innovative products like our 100% bison and elk sticks to more consumers, expand markets for our products, and create additional opportunities for agriculture and rural communities,” Reid added. “We appreciate USDA’s investment in small producers and rural businesses like ours, and we’re excited about what this grant will help us build.”
Source: US Department of Agriculture
USDA Rural Development’s Value-Added Producer Grant Program helps producers develop value-added agricultural products, conduct market research and implement business and marketing strategies. Applications for the Value-Added Producer Grant program are typically accepted for processing from agricultural producers between January and May, depending on when program funding is allocated, the agency said.
“Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins is highly focused on supporting American farmers and locally raised food products,” said Rural Development Utah State Director Stan Summers. “Farm Creek Meats is a great example of Utah producers strengthening our agricultural economy and supporting our nation’s goals. This investment will give the company the backing it needs to expand its reach, bring more locally raised products to market, and set themselves up for long‑term opportunities.”
Additional information on USDA Rural Development investments in rural America is available at the
Rural Data Gateway
.

news_title: Rome Grinding Solutions marks 50 years of manufacturing growth - meat+poultry

SHELDON, IOWA — Rome Grinding Solutions, a leading, family-owned, US-based industrial grinder manufacturer, marks its 50
th
anniversary in 2026.
Customers and industry leaders will have opportunities to celebrate this milestone with Rome throughout this anniversary year at PACK EXPO International 2026 in Chicago, and at IPPE 2027 in Atlanta. Rome will be showcasing its industrial grinding equipment, cutting-edge add-ons and aftermarket services throughout the year.
“What started in our family’s basement has grown into a 70,000-square-foot production facility, with patented solutions and lifelong relationships with our customers,” said Kelley J. Newgard, owner and chief financial officer, Rome Grinding Solutions. “We’re grateful for every client, team member, and partner for making this accomplishment possible. Thank you for your trust and for being a fundamental part of the Rome family’s legacy over the past five decades.”
Rome Grinding Solutions was founded in 1976 in a family basement in Ankeny, Iowa. Since 2015, Kate Rome has spearheaded the company’s development, growth and rise to industry-leading status, creating unprecedented momentum as Rome enters its fifth decade of operations, according to the company. Over 50 years, Rome has grown from offering a single service to offering four original grinder lines, securing four patents, and delivering exceptional aftermarket services, audits, training and in-house manufacturing capabilities. Rome has grown with its customers to help keep food production as safe as possible, the company said.
Source: Rome Grinding Solutions
“We believe American manufacturing matters,” said Kate Rome, chief executive officer, Rome Grinding Solutions. “It strengthens our communities, creates skilled careers, drives innovation, and allows us to deliver the quality, reliability, and service our customers depend on.
“As we begin this milestone year, we’re not focused on an exit strategy,” she added. “We’re focused on building a legacy company, one that continues investing in our people, our customers, our community, and American manufacturing while never losing sight of where we came from.”

MINNEAPOLIS — Lorissa’s Organic Snacks, a product in the Link Snacks portfolio, announced it is rolling out the product in select Target stores nationwide and online.
The meat sticks are available in various flavors including Original Beef, Jalapeño Beef and Savory Herb Turkey.

WESTMINSTER, COLO. — On Oct. 1, Niman Ranch released a report on the nutrient density of its new Regenerative Organic Certified (ROC) beef program based on published lab results. Niman Ranch commissioned the analysis and Edacious an independent ISO/IEC 17025-2017 accredited laboratory, conducted the analysis.
The results compared Niman Ranch ROC ribeye and ground beef with corresponding nutrient values in USDA FoodData Central Foundation Foods
[i]
. The findings provide an early look at how Niman Ranch’s domestic, grass-fed, regenerative organic production system may impact beef quality and nutrient density. Key insights from the analysis include:
Niman Ranch Regenerative Organic Ribeye
features 284% more Omega-3 fatty acids, a 7x more favorable Omega-6 to Omega-3 ratio, +52% Vitamin A, +38% Selenium and +20% Iron compared to the standard USDA benchmarks.
Compared to USDA Ribeye.
[ii]
Niman Ranch Regenerative Organic Ground Beef
delivers 179% more Omega-3s, 43% more ALA, +4,624% EPA, +61% Selenium, +41% Vitamin B2 and +123% Manganese.
Compared to USDA ground beef.
[iii]
While not a definitive or statistically comprehensive study, the analysis was a critical step in studying the potential nutritional advantages of beef sourced from Niman Ranch’s regenerative organic program. Niman Ranch will continue to explore further how different factors can drive meat quality.
“At Niman Ranch, we have long believed that how beef is raised fundamentally impacts meat quality and marbling,” said Nick Tarpoff, vice president of Beef Procurement and Supply Chain at Niman Ranch. “These initial findings take that belief a step further, showing how regenerative raising practices and cattle genetics may also translate to nutrition benefits.”
Health-conscious consumers continue to push the demand for beef. Shoppers increasingly look past standard macronutrients and have begun to prioritize whole, clean proteins and understand the deeper nutritional quality of their food, Niman Ranch said. The “Food Is Medicine” movement has seen consumers embrace real-food nutrient density and evaluate essential micronutrients, healthy fatty acid profiles and sustainable land management practices when choosing what to purchase.
Niman Ranch’s regenerative organic beef program carries triple certification, including Regenerative Organic Certified, USDA Organic and Certified Humane. All Niman Ranch regenerative organic cattle are born, raised and harvested in the United States by family ranchers across more than 105,000 acres opposed to an estimated 95% of organic beef and 80% of grass-fed beef sold in the United States that is imported, the company said.
“At Edacious, our mission is to bring trust and transparency to food quality by connecting the dots between soil health and human health,” said Eric Smith, founder and chief executive officer of Edacious. “Niman Ranch offers another indicator that when you manage land holistically — prioritizing soil health, animal care and premium genetics — you have the potential to elevate the nutritional density and quality of the final product.”
Niman Ranch’s regenerative organic beef is now available at Natural Grocers’ 174 locations across 22 states as well as at regional and specialty grocers including Laurel Supply, Nude Miami, Plum Market and select co-op markets throughout the West Coast.

news_title: New York farm barred from selling raw milk because of positive test for Listeria
efet_title: New York farm barred from selling raw milk because of positive test for Listeria
efet_body:
New York officials are warning the public not to consume raw milk from Big Brook Farm in Lee Center because it has tested positive for Listeria monocytogenes.
In the warning issued Sept. 30, State Agriculture and Markets Commissioner Richard A. Ball said a sample of the dairy’s milk collected by a state inspector returned the positive result. Follow-up testing confirmed the presence of the bacteria.
The farm is banned from selling raw milk until tests show it is pathogen free.
In 2024 a similar warning was issued after testing showed the farm's milk was contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes.
As of Oct. 1 no illnesses have been confirmed, but it can take up to 70 days for symptoms of Listeria infection to develop.
Raw milk, sometimes referred to as fresh milk, has not been pasteurized to kill harmful bacteria including Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and others. Research has shown that people who drink raw milk are 800 more times likely to become sick than those who drink pasteurized milk.
It is illegal to sell raw milk across state lines.
About Listeria infections
Food contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes may not look, smell or taste spoiled but can still cause serious and sometimes life-threatening infections. Anyone who has consumed any of the implicated raw milk and developed symptoms of Listeria infection should seek medical treatment and tell their doctors about the possible Listeria exposure.
Also, anyone who has eaten any of the recalled products should monitor themselves for symptoms during the coming weeks because it can take up to 70 days after exposure to Listeria for symptoms of listeriosis to develop.
Symptoms of Listeria infection can include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache, and neck stiffness. Specific laboratory tests are required to diagnose Listeria infections, which can mimic other illnesses.
Pregnant women, the elderly, young children, and people such as cancer patients who have weakened immune systems are particularly at risk of serious illnesses, life-threatening infections, other complications and death. Although infected pregnant women may experience only mild, flu-like symptoms, their infections can lead to premature delivery, infection of the newborn, or even stillbirth.

MCLEAN, VA. — The Food Production Solutions Association (FPSA) will host Cultivate: Leadership Growth Lab on November 5-6, 2026, in Lexington, Ky., bringing together early- to mid-career professionals from across the food and beverage industry for two days of hands-on leadership development, peer learning, and real-world application.
Unlike traditional leadership conferences built around presentations and lectures, Cultivate is designed as an immersive experience where participants actively practice leadership skills through simulations, facilitated discussions, team challenges, site observations, and personal reflection.
The experience begins before attendees even arrive, with a complimentary DiSC® assessment that helps participants better understand their communication style, leadership tendencies, and how they interact with others. Throughout the event, self-awareness becomes the foundation for a series of interactive leadership experiences designed to strengthen communication, influence, decision-making, collaboration, and confidence.
"Leadership isn't developed by sitting in a room and listening to someone talk about it," said Chris Lyons, President & CEO of FPSA. "Cultivate gives participants the opportunity to practice leadership, receive feedback, learn from peers, and see it in action. They will leave with tools they can immediately apply in their careers."
According to FPSA's workforce research, leadership and problem-solving skills remain among the areas organizations struggle most to develop. Cultivate was created to help address that need through practical, experience-based learning.
A Leadership Journey, Not a Conference
Over two days, participants will:
Complete a complimentary DiSC® assessment and explore how their communication style impacts leadership effectiveness
Join a small Cultivate Circle that serves as a peer learning and accountability group throughout the program
Participate in interactive leadership simulations requiring communication, collaboration, and decision-making under pressure
Practice navigating difficult workplace conversations and providing constructive feedback
Learn how to build influence and gain buy-in without relying on title or authority
Observe leadership, teamwork, and operational excellence in action during a visit to the Toyota Kentucky Experience Center
Work through real-world leadership challenges with peers and industry facilitators
Create a personal leadership action plan to apply immediately after returning to work
Throughout the program, participants will learn from a diverse group of entrepreneurs, executive coaches, leadership experts, and industry professionals, including Jason Burke, Founder of New Primal, Emma Hossack, Amy Goodson, Leslie Minchin, Donald Woolridge, and John Parke.
A highlight of the experience includes an evening reception and networking event at RD1 Distillery, where participants can continue conversations, strengthen professional relationships, and Hear from RD1's Master Distiller about how he innovates and brings new products to market.
Designed for the Next Generation of Industry Leaders
Cultivate was developed for professionals who are beginning to lead projects, influence teams, supervise others, or prepare for expanded leadership responsibilities. The program focuses on practical skills participants can use immediately, helping them become stronger communicators, more confident decision-makers, and more effective leaders.
"The goal is simple," Lyons said. "We want participants to leave with greater self-awareness, stronger leadership skills, and a network of peers they can continue learning from long after the event ends."
Sponsorship and Registration Information
Organizations looking to support the development of emerging leaders while increasing their visibility within the food and beverage industry can explore a variety of Cultivate sponsorship opportunities. WASHINGTON — The Trump Administration recently nominated Greg Ibach as the next undersecretary for trade and foreign agricultural affairs.

The Meat Institute also announced its support of Ibach’s nomination and its impact on meat businesses across the United States.
“Greg Ibach is a committed public servant with deep knowledge of agricultural markets, and he understands that access to new markets is especially critical to beef and pork producers and processors,” said Julie Anna Potts, president and chief executive officer for Meat Institute. “Ibach’s appointment will advance the Trump Administration’s ongoing efforts to break down tariff and non-tariff barriers in global markets to enable the US meat and poultry industry to benefit from expanded demand for high-quality, nutritious American meat and poultry products.”

in negotiations with China, the Meat Institute celebrated beef and pork’s inclusion on the list.
“The Meat Institute is appreciative of Ambassador Greer’s ongoing efforts to secure greater access to Chinese markets for US pork and beef,” said Julie Anna Potts, president and chief executive officer of the Meat Institute. “It was great to see the inclusion of beef and pork on the list of non-sensitive goods, which will set the foundation for addressing persistently high retaliatory tariffs and trade-limiting non-tariff barriers on US meat exports. This was one of the Meat Institute’s requests, and we thank the Trump administration for its dedication to securing more favorable access for our exports.”
China is a key market for the US beef supply chain, particularly for US beef variety meats and offal, which hold minimal demand in the United States compared to strong prices in China.
“These US beef exports to China support higher carcass values and reduce price pressure on domestic cuts, contributing to more stable beef prices for American consumers,” Potts explained. “Strong export demand drives higher carcass value, which encourages cattle producers in the US to rebuild the herd.”
The Meat Institute said it was also encouraged by the technical agricultural working group established under the Board of Trade.
“We look forward to continuing to work with the Trump administration to ensure that outstanding issues impeding beef trade to China, including ongoing plant suspensions that violate the spirit of the Phase One Agreement, be addressed when this working group meets later this year,” Potts said.
In May 2026, China began to
renew expired registrations
for some US beef facilities, improving access to the market. However, other limitations have hindered the US beef industry’s trade with China.
Several US beef plants were delisted after first-offense detections of ractopamine or melengestrol acetate (MGA), contrary to the Phase One Agreement, noted the Meat Institute. The group has since called for China to align its ractopamine policy with the agreement and implement a clear, transparent and enforceable process to prevent plants suspended for MGA or ractopamine findings from being barred indefinitely.
“While we know these negotiations take time, we are confident Ambassador Greer and Ambassador Callahan will continue to work on the remaining, highly technical non-tariff barriers which continue to hinder access to China,” Potts said.

Meat Snacks Are Moving Into the Mainstream
Once a convenience-store staple, meat snacks are becoming an everyday source of protein. As consumers seek convenient, satisfying options across more eating occasions, the category is expanding well beyond its traditional roots.
U.S. meat snack sales have grown more than 45% over the past four years to $4.4 billion, according to CoBank1. Circana data shows meat snacks generated $6.7 billion in sales for the 52 weeks ending May 17, 2026, up 11.8% year over year2.
But growth brings competition. Protein and convenience may bring consumers to the category, but flavor and the ingredient statement can give them a reason to choose one product over another.

In fact, 27% of consumers seek meat snacks with new flavors or variety while also looking for products made natural ingredients, according to Mintel3. This creates a fundamental challenge: How can meat snacks deliver a simpler ingredient story without compromising what the finished product needs to deliver?
Flavor is Becoming a Key Point of Differentiation
Flavor can be a powerful driver of trial. According to Innova Market Insights, 38% of U.S. and Canadian consumers say a flavor that is new to them would make them interested in trying a new snack. Balanced nutritional content follows at 29%, while 28% cite minimal processing4.
That appetite for something new is already influencing meat snack innovation. Mintel notes that meat and protein snack brands are borrowing from Asian flavors to deliver “bolder heat,” using Asian-inspired sweet-and-spicy profiles to add complexity to a category long dominated by traditional flavors.
For brands, global-inspired profiles, bold heat and unexpected sweet-and-savory combinations can create new reasons to try the category.
“Flavor innovation is about more than finding a flavor that sounds exciting. You have to understand how that flavor will perform within the finished product and how it interacts with the cure, processing and overall formulation,” says Broghan Heron, Marketing Manager at Vibrant Ingredients™.
That is where flavor and cure expertise intersect. The right flavor needs to complement the formulation and processing conditions, not simply stand out on the concept sheet.

Traditional curing ingredients such as sodium nitrite, nitrate and sodium erythorbate perform specific functions in meat formulations. Natural curing approaches can use plant-derived ingredients to provide important functionality while supporting a more recognizable ingredient story.
Cultured celery, for example, can provide a natural source of nitrite for the curing process and may be as celery powder or cultured celery powder, depending on the formulation and applicable labeling requirements.
Acerola cherry provides a natural source of ascorbic acid that can help accelerate the curing reaction and support consistent cured color development. It can also contribute antioxidant functionality during processing, supporting finished-product quality.

But natural cure is not a one-for-one ingredient swap. Brands have to understand how the complete formulation performs across food safety and curing, color development and stability, flavor and sensory performance, shelf life and consistency, processing and scalability, and regulatory and labeling requirements.
For meat snack brands, that complexity is where formulation expertise becomes critical.
Vibrant Ingredients is the original creator of natural cure solutions and is one of only two manufacturers permitted to sell natural cure in the United States and Canada. Its expertise spans natural curing technology, formulation and application.

efet_body:
AUSTIN, MINN. — Hormel Foods Corp. is acquiring Brakebush Brothers LLC, Westfield, Wis., a processor of value-added chicken, for approximately $1.06 billion.
“Brakebush is a highly respected leader in value-added chicken and has earned the trust of customers for more than 100 years through innovation, quality and exceptional relationships,” said Jeff Ettinger, interim chief executive officer of Hormel Foods. “The company’s talented team, strong culture and differentiated capabilities make it an excellent fit for Hormel Foods. Our industry-leading Foodservice business has been a source of growth, and we are excited to meaningfully expand our presence in value-added chicken.”
Hormel’s Foodservice business unit
has been a bright spot for the company recently. The business generates approximately one-third of Hormel’s sales and half of its profits.
“Chicken has been one of the most attractive growth categories in protein, and Brakebush has built an exceptional platform to serve that demand,” said John Ghingo, president and CEO-elect of Hormel. “Hormel Foods has built a strong Foodservice business by helping operators succeed through innovation, service and value-added solutions. We believe that Brakebush will bolster our capabilities, bringing additional scale, expertise and customer reach, in support of our long-term growth strategy.”
Brakebush, which was founded in 1925, generated approximately $1.2 billion in net sales over the last 12 months, according to Hormel Foods, and operates five manufacturing facilities and two research and development labs.
“Brakebush has always been a people-first company, built on strong relationships, shared values and a commitment to doing business the right way,” said Carey Brakebush, chairman of the board for Brakebush. “We see those same qualities in Hormel Foods. Their culture, integrity and long-term approach to growth give us great confidence that Brakebush will continue to thrive for our employees, customers and communities in the years ahead.”

Evan Arndt, owner of Stoney Point Premium Snacks, Littlestown, Pa., carries four generations of butchers’ blood. Arndt’s great grandfather began the legacy by starting a butcher shop in the Pennsylvania borough of East Berlin. There were two sons, Wayne and Evan Arndts’s grandfather, Charlie Nell, who carried on the trade and started another butcher shop as partners in the mid-1950s. The Nell brothers split and in 1980 Arndt’s grandfather moved to Littlestown to start his own shop that became Stoney Point Farm Market. Arndt’s mother, Michelle, worked in the shop, then in 1986 his father, Bruce Arndt, began work at the shop.
“So, I literally grew up in a butcher shop more or less the whole way through,” Arndt said. “I grew up working on the kill floor, trimming, doing deer processing. So, the butchering end of it was always in my blood.”
In 1997, Arndt’s grandparents sold the butcher shop, Arndt was 13 years old with a sister two years older. Arndt’s parents stayed on and worked for the new owner for roughly seven years. The new ownership took the business in the direction of lower cost, cheaper product in greater quantity, rather than the high-quality the family had sold in the past.
“We had a retail store in the front and processing in the back,” Arndt said. “And over those seven years is when my dad got very tired of working for somebody that he saw ruining the company, bringing the company down.”
In April 2000, Bruce Arndt took a pivotal step that changed everything. He read the entrepreneurial and personal finance classic, “Rich Dad Poor Dad: What the Rich Teach Their Kids About Money that the Poor and Middle Class Do Not!” by Robert Kiyosaki. Then he gave the book to Evan, and he read it.
“I was 14, something like that at that point,” Arndt said. “He gave me the book and said, ‘listen, I am tired of working for somebody else and for other people’s dreams. I really want to start something with the family.’ And from there, it morphed within about six months.”
Evan Arndt's grandparents started the original butcher shop in Littlestown in 1980. (Source: Stoney Point Premium Snacks)
New chapter
While Bruce and Michelle Arndt still worked at the original butcher shop for the new ownership in 2001, they managed to buy a jerky shop from a gentleman named Earl who brought jerky under the brand of Stoney Point Jerky into the butcher shop and sold it out of a jar at the retail counter. Then in 2004, they were able to purchase the original butcher shop, and the family business came to fruition.
“By 2004, the gentleman that owned the butcher shop could not make payments anymore on the property,” Arndt said. “And my grandma, being the business savvy person that she was, held the whole entire note of the building. So on April Fool’s Day, 2004, we [Bruce and Michelle Arndt] ended up buying the butcher shop from my grandma after the other gentleman had lost it.”
By 2020, The Stoney Point Farm Market, the butcher shop and retail store, and Stoney Point Premium Snacks, the jerky business, split into separate businesses. Evan took over the jerky business, and his sister took the butcher shop and market. It all happened in tandem with COVID and Arndt had a gut feeling about what was ahead for the market.
“I was coming back from Cincinnati, and I remember vividly watching the TV screen and it was going over COVID and what it was going to do to different markets,” he said. “They said the beef market’s going to drop because no restaurants are going to be open. I remember calling my dad and I said, ‘Hey, I’m going to go ahead and buy out three to four months’ worth of meat. I honestly think the price is going to go up, not down.’ We bought that product and it was no later than about six weeks and everything went through the absolute rooftops from $3.50 to $6, or more. We had product to produce.”
The purchase put Stoney Point Premium in a position to provide product when other processors cut back or stopped altogether. Stoney Point Premium and Sheetz, the Mid-Atlantic gas and convenience chain, agreed on a large contract. Stoney Point’s Bronco Billy brand, purchased in the early 2010s from the Curry family, began to grow rapidly. Stoney Point’s products then ended up in Wawa and Rutter’s convenience chains.
“I want to say 2019, we were doing maybe right around $3 million, and then that kind of breaks us into the $6 million, $7 million mark,” Arndt said. “So, this year, we’re looking at $15 million with what we’re taking on. We should be hitting $20 million or more going into next year.”
With that type of business growth comes the need for physical facility capability growth. In 2001, Stoney Point Premium’s original jerky facility was approximately 100 square feet. The Arndts rebuilt the family garage taking it from 300 square feet to 1,100 square feet for jerky production.

KANSAS CITY, MO. — Americans are redefining what dinner means. For an increasing number, it means smaller meals that fall somewhere between a snack and a traditional meal. It may even occur during a beefed-up version of happy hour, where drinks are supplemented with appetizers and other small portions.
It’s all a perfect fit for imported deli meats from Italy, Spain and other countries.
The US market for Italian cured meats has evolved significantly in recent years, said Claudia Biagiotti, e-commerce manager for Sogno Toscano.
American consumers are becoming more knowledgeable and adventurous, with growing interest not only in prosciutto but also in specialties, such as mortadella, bresaola, guanciale, finocchiona, coppa, capocollo, speck, culatello and ’nduja.
“The popularity of cured meats in the US encouraged us to expand our offering beyond Italy, introducing selected Spanish salumi and French-inspired duck specialties alongside our Italian assortment,” Biagiotti said. “Consumers are increasingly interested in discovering where these products come from, how they’re made and the traditions behind them.”
This growing curiosity and appreciation for European charcuterie has allowed Sogno Toscano to continue expanding its selection while remaining focused on quality, authenticity and craftsmanship.
Charcuterie boards, focaccia and premium Italian cured meats are winning over American consumers as demand grows for conviviality, quality and authentic shared experiences, according to Veroni.
“Italian tradition continues to rank among America’s favorite food trends,” Veroni said. “In the United States, happy hour is no longer just a quick after-work drink. No longer limited to cocktails and snacks, it has evolved into a ritual centered on quality, flavor, conviviality and sharing.

For 63%, it’s primarily an opportunity to relax and unwind, while nearly one-third prefer enjoying happy hour at home, turning it into a social occasion shared with friends and family.
“In this evolving landscape, the symbols of Italian conviviality are taking center stage; charcuterie boards, focaccia, pinsa, sheet-pan pizza and schiacciata become the choice to be shared among friends and family,” according to Veroni.
The aperitivo economy
Simple yet flavorful foods that reflect a culinary culture built around authentic ingredients and moments of togetherness. efet_title: Walmart discusses shifts for healthier options - meat+poultry
efet_body:
LAS VEGAS — PepsiCo, Walmart and Unilever executives say changing health behaviors are creating new opportunities – and new risks – for brands and retailers.
A pair of presentations at Groceryshop on Sept. 23 in Las Vegas highlighted evolving consumer attitudes around wellness and how they are transforming the future of food.
At Walmart, about one in six shoppers is shifting towards healthier choices, said Brett Wein, vice president of food at Walmart Connect. These transitions could erode brand loyalty by as much as 52%, he said.
PepsiCo is responding by expanding its portfolio to meet demand for products with functional benefits, different nutritional attributes and smaller portion sizes, said Nicolle Poole, vice president of shopper marketing for Walmart at PepsiCo.
“Health and wellness means a lot of different things to a lot of different shoppers,” she said. “And so what we really want to do is make sure that consumers have choice.”
Changing health behaviors also are reshaping PepsiCo’s marketing strategy. Rather than relying solely on broad audience segments such as the “health-conscious consumer,” Poole said the company is layering in more nuanced targeting based on shopper data and behavioral insights.
“When you look at those consumers making lifestyle shifts, there are some leading indicators within the data that tell us these people are more likely to be someone that is making a change that could be in that 52% that we lose,” Poole said.
Identifying those signals earlier gives PepsiCo an opportunity to introduce shoppers to products that meet their changing needs before they abandon the portfolio. Acting quickly on those insights, however, requires collaboration across sales, marketing, insights and other functions, Poole said.
From reactive to proactive
The forces driving changing health behaviors extend well beyond traditional notions of dieting.
In a separate Groceryshop presentation, Jostein Solheim, chief executive officer of Unilever Wellbeing, outlined three significant shifts reshaping how consumers think about health. Those changes have helped drive Unilever’s investments in vitamin and supplement brands spanning hydration, digestive health, sleep support, hair growth and other needs.
The first shift he described is the evolution of health from the absence of disease to an everyday lifestyle. Consumers are increasingly becoming active participants in managing their health rather than reacting to a problem.
Secondly, beauty and wellbeing are covering. Solheim said nine in 10 consumers view these concepts as interconnected.
“Eighty-six percent of consumers say you can’t feel beautiful if you’re not feeling good inside,” he said.
The third major shift is the democratization of health information. Consumers today have unprecedented access to information about ingredients, nutrition and scientific research, which allows them to take a more active role in managing their health.
The rising adoption of GLP-1 weight loss medications is accelerating that movement, Solheim said. Reduced food intake puts a greater emphasis on nutrient density, creating opportunities for products positioned around protein, fiber, micronutrients and hydration.
And, increasingly, consumers aren’t waiting until later in life to focus on their health.
“The whole wellbeing industry is driven by Gen Zs,” Solheim said. “It was Millennials and now Gen Zs. They are disproportionately engaging, investing and thankfully educating the elders,” he said.
That could expand the market for wellness products as younger consumers look beyond addressing existing concerns and seek to prevent future health problems.
For manufacturers and retailers, the opportunity may extend beyond simply offering more products positioned as healthy. As consumers increasingly shop around specific needs, brands must identify those changing priorities early, provide products that address them and clearly communicate credible benefits.
And with brand loyalty becoming more vulnerable when consumers change their habits, the companies that recognize those shifts early may become part of shoppers’ new routines.

G. L. Mezzetta Inc. is voluntarily recalling a certain lot number of Mezzetta GOLDEN GREEK PEPERONCINI MEDIUM HEAT, 32-ounce, due to concerns of a potential pest contaminant in the jar, an alert from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said.

A video posted to TikTok circulated earlier this month and now has over 230,000 views shows what appears to be a rodent floating in the jar of peppers. "Here with the pot roast I wanted to make, Mississippi style, but there's a dead baby mouse, there's a dead baby mouse in my pepperoncini's," a woman in the video says in part.
Read More
on
News
There have been no reported illnesses or injuries related to the recall, the alert notes. No other products are included in the recall.
Newsweek
reached out to G. L. Mezzetta Inc. via email on Monday night for comment.
...
What To Know
According to the alert,
the recall only impacts GOLDEN GREEK PEPERONCINI MEDIUM HEAT, 32 oz., with a lot number of 720106 and SKU number of 10106328. The alert says the company has identified where the recalled product was distributed and the customers who received the product.
The alert says the company is "working directly with them to isolate and remove the affected product from sale."
The product referenced in the original consumer report has been requested to be retrieved and analyzed to review sanitation and food safety records as well as the relevant production, the alert says.
People who have purchased the recalled peppers are urged not to consume them and to contact the company via email at CustomerSupport@Mezzetta.com.
Numerous recalls have been issued this year across the country due to the potential for damage, foodborne illness, contamination, lack of inspection or undeclared food allergens. Recently, federal officials also announced a recent recall from Star Meat Delivery Inc. impacting about 167,639 pounds of
raw beef, pork and goat
because the goods were produced without federal inspection.
The latest recall impacting the jarred peperoncini comes amid heightened fears and attention to foodborne illnesses and recalls,
including national cases of salmonella
and
cyclospora.
Keith Schneider, professor of food safety at the UF Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, said in a release sent to
Newsweek
earlier this month when asked if the number of food recalls and foodborne outbreaks taking place
recently has increased from past numbers, "Not necessarily."
"We tend to hear about them much more often because we have much greater access to information. We now have 24-hour news and social media, so when there is an outbreak or recall, people can hear about it repeatedly throughout the day. An actual news report can go viral, but so can information from someone who may not understand food safety or the science behind an outbreak," Schneider said.
"That can make it feel like we are seeing an unprecedented number of outbreaks when, in reality, many of the same foodborne pathogens and types of outbreaks have occurred for years. The reality is that we get an estimated 1.2 million cases of salmonella every year, which averages about 100,000 cases a month. There are about 20 million cases of norovirus each year. So, the numbers we’re seeing this summer are not out of the ordinary. The large number of cyclospora cases is unusually high for that organism. On average, we typically see 1,000 to 2,000 cases each year, so more than 20,000 cases is concerning," he added.

This story was
originally published
by
KFF Health News
.
By Stephanie Armour
The run-up to the midterm elections is turning into a food fight — literally.
The summer was marred by a massive foodborne outbreak that
sickened scores of people
and the recall of
tens of thousands of pounds
of imported meat, turning the safety of the U.S. food supply into a topic of national conversation and a political cause.
Late-night talk show hosts
joked about symptoms
that included explosive diarrhea. As a precaution,
chain restaurants
such as Chipotle and Taco Bell
yanked lettuce
, jalapeños, and other suspected products from menus. Some food safety scientists
blamed the outbreaks
on federal cuts to public health.
These dynamics collectively have raised questions about whether it’s safe to order a salad or burger.
Democrats have come out on the offensive, saying voters worried about the safety of the U.S. food supply should oust Republicans in the midterm elections. The Trump administration has countered by accusing Democrats of scaremongering over food safety to score political points.
The political fracas reflects the toll that large-scale outbreaks have had on the public psyche. Midterm voters have long cared about pocketbook issues such as grocery prices, but the spate of recalls has them worried about whether the food they’re buying is safe to eat — and political leaders are paying attention.
The outbreak linked to cyclospora in lettuce led to almost 20,000 laboratory-confirmed cases of illness from May through August, compared with 1,180 cases during the same span in 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That makes it the largest recorded outbreak of the parasite.
“One of the reasons food safety is in the news this year, and people have been rightfully concerned, is the combination of high-profile restaurant names and the absolute colossal number of illnesses,” said
Teresa Murray
, consumer watchdog director with the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, or PIRG, an advocacy group, referring to a recent cyclosporiasis outbreak. “It’s thousands of people. It makes it more real.”
Data shows
there have been about
200 food recalls
so far in 2026
, which is about on par
with the number
at this time last year, according to PIRG data.
Following the numbers
A majority of registered voters have little or no confidence in government oversight of food safety, with Democrats far more likely than Republicans to doubt the protections in place,
according to a July survey
by Quinnipiac University.
Ninety-four percent
of U.S. adults indicated they were concerned about the frequency of food recalls in a poll by GS1 US, a data standards organization.
The share of consumers who strongly agree that the U.S. food system produces food that’s safe to eat declined to about 30% in August, from 40% in November,
based on survey data
released in September by the University of Illinois and Purdue University.
Democrats have jumped at the chance to repeat criticisms of President Donald Trump’s budget cuts and priorities.
The Democratic National Committee
recently posted a list of recalled food items
on social media while calling Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. a “complete disaster” who must resign.
“Trump is dismantling our government — and it’s harming people,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) posted
Sept. 2 on the social platform X
, adding: “Slashed food safety agencies → cyclospora outbreak.” Just weeks earlier, she had written to Kennedy demanding answers for what she described as the administration’s “
failed response
” and its connection to political contributions.
Rep. Gabe Amo (D-R.I.)
posted Sept. 5 on X
: “I’m calling on Trump to stop gutting the FDA & restore its inspectors. We deserve safe food.”
The campaign for Rep. Judy Chu (D-Calif.)
posted Sept. 5 on X
: “Trump is cutting our food safety funding and workforce, and we have seen far too many food recalls this summer.”
But the number of recalls doesn’t tell the whole story.
While recalls aren’t markedly up this year compared with 2025, they are up over a broader time span. The country saw 320 food recalls by the Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture in 2025, up from 296 in 2024,
according to PIRG
.
The total number of recalls grew 21% from 2021 to 2025, based on an
analysis by Trace One
, a provider of regulatory guidance software. A rise in Class I recalls, which are the highest priority because the products could cause serious illness or death, drove much of the increase.
But recall numbers can be misleading. For starters, federal agencies do not publicize all recalls, especially if products are no longer on the market. Recall data itself is suspect because a single contaminated food can result in multiple recalls if the item is incorporated into processed food or other products.
A far better measure is the number of people sickened, epidemiologists say. And this summer’s specific multistate outbreak…[truncated]
